verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} signs{H5251} and wonders{H6381}, great{H1419}, in the heavens{H8064}; for seven{H7651} messengers{H4397} were coming{H935}, and to them were the seven{H7651} last{H314} plagues{H5061}, for in them was completed{H3615} the burning{H2740} anger{H639} from YHWH{H3068}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses the OT pair נִסִּים וְנִפְלָאוֹת ('signs and wonders') — echoing the Exodus plague formula (Deut 6:22, 26:8, 34:11, Jer 32:20-21, Neh 9:10). Greek has singular σημεῖον μέγα καὶ θαυμαστόν ('a sign, great and marvelous'). The Hebrew naturally reaches for the classic two-word pair; the Greek has a single sign with two adjectives. A back-translator from Greek would write אוֹת גְּדוֹלָה וְנִפְלָאָה (singular 'sign'), not the plural pair ניסים ונפלאות.

Uses חֲרוֹן אַף ('burning anger,' H2740 + H639) — the specific OT compound phrase for YHWH's fierce wrath, appearing over 40 times in the Tanakh (Ex 32:12, Num 25:4, Deut 13:17, Josh 7:26, 2 Kings 23:26, Ps 85:3, Isa 13:9, 13:13, Jer 4:8, 12:13, 25:37, 30:24, Lam 1:12, Nah 1:6, Zeph 2:2). Greek uses the single generic word θυμός ('wrath/fury'). A back-translator from Greek θυμός would use חֵמָה (chemah) or זַעַם (za'am), not the specific two-word compound חרון אף. The compound carries physical imagery: חרון is 'burning heat' and אף is literally 'nostril' — the flushed face of fury.
greek_deviations: Hebrew has plural נִסִּים וְנִפְלָאוֹת ('signs and wonders'). Greek has singular σημεῖον ('one sign').
Greek adds ἄλλο ('another') — absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: חרון אף מיהוה ('burning anger from YHWH'). Greek: θυμὸς τοῦ θεοῦ ('wrath of God'). Different divine name and different wrath expression.
translation_notes: 'Signs and wonders' for nisim v'nifla'ot — preserving the classic Exodus pair. The word נס (nes, H5251) in the OT means 'signal/banner/sign'; the 'miracle' sense developed in post-biblical Hebrew, but the pairing with נפלאות anchors it in the Exodus tradition.
'Burning anger' for charon af — a two-word phrase that cannot be reduced to a single English word. The compound is so distinctively Hebraic that its presence alone argues against back-translation.
The consonantal כלא is read as כָּלָה (kalah, H3615 — 'was completed/finished'). The aleph in the source pointing may reflect Aramaic orthographic influence.
textual_notes: The 'signs and wonders' formula (אותות ומופתים / ניסים ונפלאות) is the signature phrase of the Exodus plagues (Deut 6:22, 26:8, 34:11). The seven last plagues of Revelation are presented as a new Exodus — YHWH's final deliverance.
The square brackets [ ] in the source text between השבעה and נגעים indicate an editorial lacuna — a word may be missing from the source manuscript.

verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} as it were a sea{H3220} of flask, mixed{H1101} with fire{H784}; and those who overcame{H5329} the beast{H2416} and its graven-image{H6459}, standing{H5975} beside{H681} the sea{H3220} of flask; and to them were lyres{H3658} of YHWH{H3068}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses צְלוֹחִית (tselochit — 'flask/vial') — a concrete Hebrew vessel word — where Greek has ὑαλίνην (hualinen — 'of glass,' a material adjective). A back-translator from Greek 'glass' would use זְכוּכִית (zechuchit — 'glass'), not צלוחית (flask). The Hebrew sees a sea that resembles a translucent vessel; the Greek sees a sea made of glass as a material. Same distinctive word as in Rev 21:21.

Uses פֶסֶל (pesel — 'graven image,' H6459) — the EXACT word from the Second Commandment: לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה לְּךָ פֶסֶל (Ex 20:4, Deut 5:8 — 'You shall not make for yourself a graven image'). Greek uses εἰκών (eikon — 'image'), a neutral term. A back-translator from εἰκών would use צֶלֶם (tselem — 'image') or תְּמוּנָה (temunah — 'likeness'), NOT the Decalogue's specific idolatry term פסל. The Hebrew author condemns the beast's image with the Torah's own vocabulary for prohibited idol-making.

Uses כִּנּוֹרוֹת (kinnorot — 'lyres,' H3658) — David's instrument (1 Sam 16:23, 2 Sam 6:5, Ps 33:2, 137:2, 150:3), THE instrument of Israelite worship. Greek κιθάρα is the Greek lyre. More significantly, the Hebrew says כִּנּוֹרוֹת יהוה ('lyres of YHWH') — instruments belonging to YHWH, echoing 2 Chr 7:6 (כְּלֵי שִׁיר יהוה — 'instruments of song of YHWH') and 1 Chr 16:42. A back-translator from κιθάρας τοῦ θεοῦ ('harps of God') would not independently produce the Davidic/Levitical term kinnor paired with the tetragrammaton.
greek_deviations: Greek adds καὶ ἐκ τοῦ χαράγματος αὐτοῦ ἐκ τοῦ ἀριθμοῦ τοῦ ὀνόματος αὐτοῦ ('and from his mark, from the number of his name') — two additional elements absent from the more concise Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'its graven-image' (פסל — Decalogue term). Greek: 'his image' (εἰκών — neutral). Different vocabulary with vastly different theological loading.
Hebrew: 'lyres of YHWH.' Greek: 'harps of God' (κιθάρας τοῦ θεοῦ). Different instrument name and different divine name.
translation_notes: 'Flask' for tselochit — a concrete vessel word, not a material description. The sea resembles a translucent vessel, not a sea made of glass as substance.
'Graven-image' for pesel — preserving the Decalogue connection. This is the specific word Moses commanded Israel to smash (Deut 7:5, 12:3).
The square brackets [ ] in the source text before ים suggest an editorial lacuna — a modifier may be missing.
אֵצֶל (etsel, H681 — 'beside/next to') — the same intimate proximity word from Rev 21:3. Expresses physical nearness, not the generic 'upon' (ἐπί) of the Greek.
textual_notes: The overcomers standing beside the sea with lyres echoes Israel standing at the Red Sea after the Exodus (Ex 14:30-15:1). Miriam took a tambourine (Ex 15:20); here they take lyres. The sea of flask mixed with fire is the antitype of the Red Sea.
The phrase 'lyres of YHWH' echoes the Levitical worship context: 2 Chr 7:6, 1 Chr 16:42. The overcomers worship with YHWH's own dedicated instruments.

verses.translation: And making music{H2167} the song{H7892} of Moshe{H4872}, and the song{H7892} of the lamb{H7716}, and saying{H559}: Great{H1419} are your works{H4639}, YHWH{H3068} Elohei{H430} of the Hosts{H6635}! Righteous{H6664} and true{H571} are your ways{H1870}, King{H4428} of kings{H4428}!

one_way_hebrew: Uses TWO DIFFERENT Hebrew words for 'song': שִׁירָה (shirah — feminine) for Moses and שִׁיר (shir — masculine) for the Lamb. The feminine שירה is the specific term used for the Song of the Sea — Deuteronomy 31:19,22,30 and 32:44 call it הַשִּׁירָה הַזֹּאת ('this song,' feminine). Greek uses the same word ᾠδή for both. A back-translator from Greek, seeing the same word both times, would use the same Hebrew word both times. The Hebrew author deliberately connects Moses' song to the Exodus triumph at the Red Sea through the feminine form.

CRITICAL: Hebrew has מֶלֶךְ הַמְּלָכִים ('King of kings') — a native Hebrew/Aramaic royal title (Dan 2:37, Ezra 7:12). Greek TR has ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν ἁγίων ('King of saints'); other manuscripts read τῶν ἐθνῶν ('of nations') or τῶν αἰώνων ('of ages'). NO Greek manuscript reads τῶν βασιλέων ('of kings') in this verse. A back-translator from ANY Greek variant would not produce מלך המלכים. The Hebrew title independently matches Rev 17:14 and 19:16 where even the Greek has βασιλεὺς βασιλέων. The Hebrew preserves the consistent title throughout; the Greek fractures it into different readings at different points.

Uses מְזַמְּרִים (mezamrim — 'making music,' from zamar H2167) — a Psalms verb specifically meaning 'to sing praises with instruments' (Ps 21:13, 57:7, 98:5, 105:2, 108:1, 147:7, 149:3). Greek ᾄδουσιν (adousin) is generic 'singing.' The Hebrew verb implies instrumental accompaniment — consistent with the kinnorot (lyres) in the previous verse. The Greek loses the connection between instrument and song.

Uses יהוה אֱלֹהֵי הַצְּבָאוֹת ('YHWH Elohei of the Hosts') — the specific OT military-divine name (1 Sam 1:3, 4:4, 17:45, Isa 1:24, 5:16, 6:3, Jer 2:19, Amos 4:13). Greek has Κύριε ὁ θεὸς ὁ παντοκράτωρ ('Lord God Almighty'). A back-translator from Greek would write אֲדֹנָי אֱלֹהִים שַׁדַּי or similar — not the specific compound name YHWH Tsevaot which carries the military sense of YHWH commanding heavenly armies.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: מלך המלכים ('King of kings'). Greek TR: 'King of saints' (τῶν ἁγίων). Other Greek witnesses: 'King of nations' (τῶν ἐθνῶν) or 'King of ages' (τῶν αἰώνων). None match the Hebrew.
Greek adds μεγάλα καὶ θαυμαστά ('great AND marvelous'). Hebrew has only גדולה ('great') without 'marvelous.'
Greek adds τοῦ δούλου τοῦ θεοῦ ('the servant of God') after Moses — absent from the Hebrew, which simply says 'of Moshe.'
translation_notes: 'Making music' for mezamrim — capturing the instrumental-plus-vocal nature of zamar, distinct from generic singing. The overcomers play and sing simultaneously.
'Song' translates both shirah and shir in English, but the Hebrew distinction is theologically loaded: shirah (fem.) is the Exodus triumph genre; shir (masc.) is the general song form.
The song shifts from third to second person: 'works of YHWH' then 'your ways' — a typical Psalmic address pattern (enallage), where YHWH is both described and directly addressed.
textual_notes: The Song of Moses (שירת משה) refers to Exodus 15:1-18, the triumph at the Red Sea. By pairing it with the Lamb's song, the Hebrew author presents the final eschatological victory as a new Exodus.

Psalm 111:2 — גְּדֹלִים מַעֲשֵׂי יהוה ('great are the works of YHWH'). Psalm 86:8-10 — 'All nations shall come and worship before you... you are great and do wondrous things.' The song's content is woven from Psalms.
Psalm 145:17 — צַדִּיק יהוה בְּכָל דְּרָכָיו ('Righteous is YHWH in all his ways'). The phrase 'righteous and true are your ways' echoes this Psalm directly.

verses.translation: And who{H4310} shall not fear{H3372} before{H6440} you, and give{H5414} praise{H7623} to your name{H8034}? For you{H859} alone{H905} are holy{H6918}. For all{H3605} the peoples{H5971} shall come{H935} and bow down{H7812} before{H6440} you, for your judgments{H4941} have been revealed{H1540}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שֶׁבַח (shebach — 'praise,' from shabach H7623) — a native Hebrew praise verb found in the Psalms (63:4, 117:1, 145:4, 147:12) and Ecclesiastes (4:2, 8:15). Greek has δοξάσει ('glorify'). A back-translator from δοξάζω would use כִּבֵּד (kived — 'glorify/honor') or פֵּאֵר (pe'er — 'glorify'), not the distinctively Hebrew שבח.

Uses נִתְגַּלָּה (nitgalah — 'have been revealed/uncovered,' from galah H1540) — a reflexive form meaning 'became uncovered/disclosed.' The root גלה carries uniquely Hebrew connotations: it is the same root as גָּלוּת (galut — 'exile') and means to 'strip bare/uncover/exile.' Greek has ἐφανερώθησαν ('were made manifest'). A back-translator would use נוֹדְעוּ (nod'u — 'became known'), not galah with its distinctive Hebrew exile/uncovering semantic range.

Echoes Psalm 86:9 nearly verbatim: כָּל גּוֹיִם אֲשֶׁר עָשִׂיתָ יָבוֹאוּ וְיִשְׁתַּחֲווּ לְפָנֶיךָ ('all nations shall come and bow down before you'). The Hebrew preserves the Psalmist's exact construction יָבוֹאוּ וְיִשְׁתַּחֲוֻ לְפָנֶיךָ. Greek has ἥξουσιν καὶ προσκυνήσουσιν ἐνώπιόν σου — a translation, not the source. A back-translator from Greek would not independently reconstruct the Psalm's exact phrasing.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'before you' (לְפָנֶיךָ — spatial, 'before your face'). Greek: σε (accusative 'you' — direct object). Different grammatical constructions reflecting different orientations — Hebrew spatial vs. Greek relational.
Hebrew: עַמִּים ('peoples'). Greek: ἔθνη ('nations/gentiles'). Different nuance — amim is more neutral; ethne carries the gentile/pagan connotation.
translation_notes: 'Praise' for shebach — a native Hebrew praise word distinct from 'glorify.' The Hebrew concept of shebach is specifically vocal declaration of praise.
'Revealed' for nitgalah preserves the galah root's primary sense of uncovering what was hidden — YHWH's judgments were concealed and are now laid bare.
textual_notes: Echoes Jeremiah 10:7 — מִי לֹא יִרָאֲךָ מֶלֶךְ הַגּוֹיִם ('Who would not fear you, O King of the nations?'). The Hebrew opening ומי לא יראה לפניך naturally draws on Jeremiah.

Echoes Psalm 86:9-10 — 'All nations shall come and bow down before you, O Lord, and shall glorify your name. For you are great and do wondrous things; you alone are Elohim.' The Hebrew text weaves together Jeremiah and Psalms — OT intertextuality natural to a Hebrew author.

verses.translation: And after{H310} this I saw{H7200} that the Ark{H727} of the Covenant{H1285} was opened{H6605} in the heavens{H8064}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew has אֲרוֹן הַבְּרִית ('the Ark of the Covenant,' H727 + H1285) — the most sacred object in the Tabernacle, the gold-covered chest containing the tablets of the Torah (Deut 10:8, 31:9,25-26, Josh 3:3,6, 1 Sam 4:3-4, 1 Kings 8:1,6). Greek has ὁ ναὸς τῆς σκηνῆς τοῦ μαρτυρίου ('the temple of the tabernacle of the testimony'). These are COMPLETELY different things — the ARK (a sacred chest) vs. the TEMPLE of the TABERNACLE (a structure containing it). A back-translator from Greek would write הֵיכַל מִשְׁכַּן הָעֵדוּת ('temple of the tabernacle of testimony'), NEVER ארון הברית. This is among the strongest one-way markers in the entire chapter.

Hebrew uses בְּרִית (berit — 'covenant,' H1285). Greek uses μαρτύριον ('testimony/witness'). The Ark has both associations in the OT: אֲרוֹן הַבְּרִית (Ark of the Covenant, Num 10:33, Deut 10:8, Josh 3:3) and אֲרוֹן הָעֵדוּת (Ark of the Testimony, Ex 25:22, 26:33). The Hebrew author chose the COVENANT term, emphasizing YHWH's covenant obligations being enforced through the coming plagues; the Greek reflects the TESTIMONY term. A back-translator would follow the Greek 'testimony,' not independently choose the theologically distinct 'covenant.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the Ark of the Covenant' (an object — a gold-covered chest). Greek: 'the temple of the tabernacle of the testimony' (a structure). Entirely different referent — the innermost sacred object vs. the outer sacred building.
Hebrew: בְּרִית ('covenant'). Greek: μαρτύριον ('testimony/witness'). Different theological framing of the Ark's significance.
Greek adds ἰδού ('behold!') — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Ark of the Covenant' is the standard English rendering of ארון הברית. The Ark contained the two tablets of the Torah, Aaron's rod that budded, and the jar of manna (Heb 9:4). Its opening signals the enforcement of the covenant through judgment.
textual_notes: The Ark of the Covenant disappeared when Babylon destroyed the First Temple (586 BCE). Jewish tradition holds Jeremiah hid it (2 Macc 2:4-8). The Hebrew Revelation envisions the Ark in its heavenly archetype — now opened, the covenant terms are enforced through the seven plagues.
The seven messengers emerge from the opened Ark (v.6), not from a temple. The plagues originate from the covenant itself — its violation demands its enforcement.

verses.translation: And the seven{H7651} messengers{H4397} who had the seven{H7651} plagues{H5061} went out{H3318} to the outside{H2351}; clothed{H3847} in white{H3836} garments{H4403}, with a girdle{H2290} of gold{H2091} upon their loins{H4975}.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew: girdle 'upon their loins' (עַל מָתְנֵיהֶם, H4975). Greek: 'about their chests' (περὶ τὰ στήθη). Different body location. The Hebrew priestly girdle was worn at the waist/loins — matching the priestly garments (Ex 28:4, 29:9, Lev 8:7, 16:4 — the אַבְנֵט worn at the waist). A back-translator from Greek 'chests' would write עַל חֲזֵיהֶם ('upon their chests'), not על מתניהם ('upon their loins'). The Hebrew naturally places the girdle where priestly tradition requires it.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'went out to the outside' (from the Ark, v.5). Greek: 'went out from the temple' (ἐκ τοῦ ναοῦ). Connected to the v.5 difference — the Hebrew messengers emerge from the Ark of the Covenant; the Greek messengers emerge from a temple.

Hebrew: 'white garments' (מלבושי לבנים — color description). Greek: λίνον καθαρὸν λαμπρόν ('pure bright linen' — material description). Hebrew describes what the garments looked like; Greek describes what they were made of.
Hebrew: girdle 'upon their loins.' Greek: girdle 'about their chests.' Different body placement.
translation_notes: The consonantal text for לבנים reads as לְבָנִים (levanim — 'white,' from lavan H3836). The source vowel pointing (לְבֵינִים) appears irregular and may reflect scribal confusion with לְבֵנִים ('bricks'); the consonantal reading 'white' is clearly correct in context.

'Girdle' for chagor (H2290) — a belt or sash used in both priestly and military contexts (1 Sam 18:4, 2 Sam 20:8). The golden girdle on the loins presents the messengers as priestly figures executing covenant judgment.
textual_notes: The imagery of messengers emerging from the Ark of the Covenant carrying plagues echoes the Ark's fearsome power in the OT: the Ark brought plagues upon the Philistines (1 Sam 5:6-12), struck down Uzzah for unauthorized contact (2 Sam 6:7), and preceded Israel's armies into battle (Num 10:33-35).
White garments with golden girdles are priestly attire — the messengers are presented as priests of the heavenly Tabernacle executing YHWH's covenant judgment.

verses.translation: And one{H259} of the four{H702} living creatures{H2416} gave{H5414} to the seven{H7651} messengers{H4397} seven{H7651} bowls{H7086} of gold{H2091}, full{H4392} of the burning anger{H2740} of YHWH{H3068}, the living one{H2416} from everlasting{H5769} and unto everlasting{H5769}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses קְעָרוֹת (ke'arot — 'bowls/dishes,' H7086) — the specific Tabernacle dedication bowls from Numbers 7. In Numbers 7:13,19,25,31,37,43,49,55,61,67,73,79,84,85, every tribal leader brought a קַעֲרַת כֶּסֶף ('silver bowl') for the altar dedication — twelve bowls to consecrate the altar. Greek uses φιάλας (phialas — generic 'vials'). A back-translator could use any bowl word; the Hebrew author chose the specific Numbers 7 altar-dedication vessels. The wrath-bowls invert the dedication pattern: what once consecrated the altar now pours out judgment.

Uses מֵעוֹלָם וְעַד עוֹלָם ('from everlasting and unto everlasting') — the classic OT doxology formula, a direct quote from Psalm 90:2 (מֵעוֹלָם עַד עוֹלָם אַתָּה אֵל — 'from everlasting to everlasting you are God'), and the closing formula of Ps 106:48 and 1 Chr 16:36. Greek has εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ('unto the ages of the ages'). These are fundamentally different temporal expressions — the Hebrew is a Psalm quotation; the Greek is the standard Greek liturgical formula. A back-translator from Greek would write לעולמי עולמים, not the Psalm 90:2 phrase.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: חרון יהוה ('burning anger of YHWH'). Greek: θυμοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ ('wrath of God'). Same pattern as v.1 — the specific OT compound phrase vs. generic Greek wrath.
Hebrew: מעולם ועד עולם ('from everlasting and unto everlasting' — Psalm 90:2). Greek: εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ('unto the ages of the ages'). Different eternal formulas.
translation_notes: 'Bowls' for ke'arot — broad offering dishes used in the Tabernacle service, not narrow vials. The connection to Numbers 7 is essential: these are altar-dedication vessels repurposed for wrath.
'From everlasting and unto everlasting' preserves the Psalm 90:2 echo — YHWH's eternality expressed in the Psalter's own language.
textual_notes: Numbers 7 records twelve tribal leaders bringing silver ke'arot (bowls) to dedicate the Tabernacle altar. The seven golden ke'arot of wrath in this verse invert and intensify the dedication pattern: silver becomes gold, twelve becomes seven (the number of completion), and what was offered for consecration is now poured out for consummation.

Psalm 90:2 — 'Before the mountains were born, or you brought forth the earth and the world, from everlasting to everlasting, you are God.' The Hebrew formula anchors YHWH's judgment in his eternal nature.

verses.translation: And the house{H1004} of prayer{H8605} was filled{H4390} with smoke{H6227}; and the glory{H3519} of YHWH{H3068} filled{H4390} the tabernacle{H4908}; and no one{H259} was able{H3201} to walk{H1980} into it until{H5704} the seven{H7651} plagues{H5061} from the seven{H7651} messengers{H4397} were completed{H3615}.

one_way_hebrew: NEAR-VERBATIM QUOTE from Exodus 40:34-35: וּכְבוֹד יהוה מָלֵא אֶת הַמִּשְׁכָּן וְלֹא יָכֹל מֹשֶׁה לָבוֹא ('and the glory of YHWH filled the tabernacle, and Moses was not able to enter'). The Hebrew Revelation has וּכְבוֹד יהוה מָלֵא אֶת הַמִּשְׁכָּן וְשׁוּם אֶחָד יוּכַל לֵילֵךְ לְתוֹכָהּ ('and the glory of YHWH filled the tabernacle, and no one was able to walk into it'). The phrase כבוד יהוה מלא את המשכן is virtually identical to Exodus 40:34. The Greek merely says ἐγεμίσθη ὁ ναὸς καπνοῦ ('the temple was filled with smoke') — losing the entire Exodus quotation. A back-translator from Greek would NEVER independently reconstruct the Exodus 40:34 phrasing.

Uses TWO different terms for sacred space: בֵּית הַתְּפִילָּה ('house of prayer,' H8605) and הַמִּשְׁכָּן ('the tabernacle,' H4908). Greek uses ναός ('temple') as the single referent for both. A back-translator from Greek, seeing one word ναός, would use the same Hebrew word both times. The Hebrew author distinguishes: the prayer-house fills with smoke; the Tabernacle fills with YHWH's glory. Same two-term pattern as Rev 21:22 where the Hebrew distinguishes בית תפילה from בית המקדש while Greek uses one word ναός.

Uses מִשְׁכָּן (mishkan — 'tabernacle/dwelling-place,' H4908) — the specific word for the Tabernacle of Moses (Ex 25:9, 26:1ff), connecting this heavenly vision directly to the Sinai Tabernacle and its construction. Greek ναός is generic 'temple.' The mishkan is YHWH's portable dwelling among his people; the naos is any temple.
greek_deviations: Hebrew distinguishes two sacred spaces: בית התפילה ('house of prayer') filled with smoke, and המשכן ('the tabernacle') filled with YHWH's glory. Greek uses ναός ('temple') as a single referent.

Hebrew: 'the glory of YHWH filled the tabernacle' (Exodus 40:34 quote). Greek: 'the temple was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power' (ἐκ τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ). Greek adds 'and from his power' — absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: כְבוֹד יהוה ('glory of YHWH'). Greek: δόξης τοῦ θεοῦ ('glory of God'). Different divine name.
translation_notes: 'House of prayer' echoes Isaiah 56:7 — 'my house shall be called a house of prayer (בֵּית תְפִלָּה) for all peoples' — which Yeshua quotes in Matt 21:13 / Mark 11:17.
'Tabernacle' for mishkan — the Sinai-specific term, connecting the heavenly scene to the wilderness Tabernacle and its dedication.
'Walk' for leilech — more specific than the Greek εἰσελθεῖν ('enter'). The Hebrew implies physically traversing sacred space.
textual_notes: Exodus 40:34-35 (exact source): וַיְכַס הֶעָנָן אֶת אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד וּכְבוֹד יהוה מָלֵא אֶת הַמִּשְׁכָּן וְלֹא יָכֹל מֹשֶׁה לָבוֹא אֶל אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד ('the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of YHWH filled the tabernacle, and Moses was not able to enter'). The Hebrew Revelation replaces 'Moses' with 'no one' — expanding the restriction from one person to all humanity.

1 Kings 8:10-11 records the same pattern at Solomon's Temple dedication: the cloud filled the house, and the priests could not stand to minister because the glory of YHWH filled the house. Both Tabernacle and Temple dedications are echoed — the pattern of glory-filling-so-that-none-can-enter is a signature of YHWH's covenant presence.

The chapter thus ends where it began: with the Tabernacle/Exodus framework. The smoke in the house of prayer and the glory in the tabernacle form a deliberate doublet — judgment (smoke) and presence (glory) simultaneously fill the heavenly sanctuary.

chapter_notes.summary: Revelation 15 in Hebrew is structured as a new Exodus. The chapter opens with 'signs and wonders' (ניסים ונפלאות — the Exodus plague formula) and closes with a near-verbatim quotation of Exodus 40:34-35 (the glory of YHWH filling the Tabernacle). Between these Exodus bookends, the overcomers stand beside the sea with lyres — mirroring Israel at the Red Sea — and sing the Song of Moses using the specific feminine form שירה that designates the Exodus triumph genre. The Hebrew uses Torah-specific vocabulary throughout: נגעים (Levitical plagues, not generic Greek πληγαί), פסל (the Decalogue's graven-image term), קערות (Numbers 7 altar-dedication bowls), כנורות (Davidic lyres), חרון אף (the OT compound for YHWH's fierce anger), מלך המלכים (King of kings), ארון הברית (Ark of the Covenant), and משכן (the Sinai Tabernacle). The most striking one-way markers are: (1) ארון הברית ('Ark of the Covenant') where Greek has 'temple of the tabernacle of testimony' — entirely different referents; (2) the Exodus 40:34 verbatim quotation in verse 8, invisible in the Greek; (3) מלך המלכים ('King of kings') against ALL Greek manuscript witnesses which read 'King of saints/nations/ages'; (4) the שירה/שיר distinction for Moses' Exodus song vs. the Lamb's song; (5) the pesel (Decalogue graven-image term) for the beast's image; and (6) the two-sacred-space distinction (בית תפילה vs. משכן) where Greek has one word (ναός) for both. The chapter presents the seven last plagues as the antitype of the Numbers 7 Tabernacle dedication: golden bowls (קערות) once brought to consecrate the altar are now filled with YHWH's חרון אף and poured out to consummate his covenant judgment.
